result:
```text
Prepare the quarterly business review deck for our leadership meeting in two weeks. We want leaders to decide whether to invest in retention or acquisition.
Assumption: the decision is where the next increment of investment returns more revenue, so a split allocation is a valid recommendation as long as the deck states it and its rationale.
Assumption: leaders need the recommendation, how uncertain it is, and what evidence would change it, all readable in the meeting.
Build every number from the raw customer and revenue exports, not from existing dashboards or summaries. Reconcile export totals to reported revenue before analysis.
Build a quarterly revenue bridge: opening revenue + new + expansion − contraction − churn = closing revenue. Report gross and net revenue retention from it.
Build cohort retention curves by acquisition quarter. Use Kaplan-Meier survival estimates for logo and revenue retention, so customers acquired recently are treated as still-active (censored) and not miscounted as retained or churned.
Compute lifetime value from survival-weighted revenue. Compute acquisition cost and payback only from authorized spend data; otherwise label the acquisition economics unverified.
Decision analysis: estimate the return on an extra dollar in retention and in acquisition. Compute the break-even retention improvement at which retention matches acquisition. Run a tornado sensitivity on the 3 to 5 inputs that move the answer most. State the recommendation and the input value that would flip it.
Write down the recommendation, the break-even value, and the decision rule before reading any held-out evidence.
Test the belief the decision rests on, that the data can tell the two returns apart. Fit retention on earlier quarters, predict the latest quarter once, and report the forecast error.
To find where churn concentrates, split customers at random at the customer level into discovery and confirmation halves, keeping all of a customer's records in one half. Search segments only in the discovery half. Check the chosen segments once in the confirmation half. Report any segment that fails confirmation as unverified.
Customer contact is prohibited, so no experiment can be run. Label every churn or growth driver as an observed association unless the past data supports a causal reading.
Red team: an existing staff member who did not build the analysis writes the strongest case for the opposite recommendation, using Analysis of Competing Hypotheses to list which evidence each option explains. One slide answers that case.
Structure the deck with the pyramid principle. Lead with the answer, and give every slide an action headline stating its claim. Draft the headlines first (a ghost deck) and confirm that the headlines alone carry the argument.
The deck is required and must be at most 12 slides. Use existing staff and tools. Do not change our operating cadence or contact customers.
With my approval only: request quarterly acquisition spend (marketing and sales cost) from the team that holds it, for acquisition cost and payback calculations.
With my approval only: deliver a separate methods-and-reconciliation note outside the 12 slides, listing data sources, calculations, the frozen decision rule, and each read of held-out evidence.
First check: the raw customer and revenue exports have been shared. They contain customer ID, start and churn dates, and revenue by period, across enough quarters to fit on earlier quarters and test on the latest. Name any missing fields or quarters.
First check: whether acquisition spend data is among the supplied artifacts. If it is absent and its request is not approved, keep acquisition economics labeled unverified.
First check: the reviewer and the red-team staff member are available before the meeting and permitted to see customer and revenue data. Existing tools can run the cohort, survival, and sensitivity analyses. When a check fails, continue only with supported, authorized work and leave the affected result unverified.
Judge: a finance or analytics staff member who did not build the deck, given the raw exports, checks that (1) the deck has at most 12 slides; (2) the headlines alone state the recommendation and the decision asked of leaders; (3) every number in the deck reproduces from the raw exports within rounding; (4) the revenue bridge reconciles opening to closing revenue each quarter; (5) the recommendation, break-even value, and flip condition match the rule written before held-out evidence was read; (6) the latest-quarter forecast error is reported, and each highlighted segment either passed the confirmation half or is labeled unverified; (7) acquisition economics use authorized spend data or are labeled unverified; (8) each driver claim is labeled association unless causally supported; (9) one slide answers the red-team case; (10) nothing in the deck requires contacting customers or changing operating cadence. Pass only if every criterion is met.
```

- `altitude`: The original outcome was a QBR deck. The improved outcome is a decision-ready deck that states the recommended allocation, the break-even value, and what would flip it, using a decision rule fixed in advance. I did not go higher to a measured pilot of either investment, because a pilot would need customer contact or a cadence change, and both are prohibited.
- `depth`: The deck is built from the raw exports, a revenue bridge, Kaplan-Meier cohort survival, and survival-weighted lifetime value instead of digested summaries. This exposes censoring errors and gives reconcilable numbers. It depends on the exports having the needed fields.
- `depth`: The belief the deck rests on is tested with a latest-quarter backtest, and churn segments are confirmed on a held-out customer half. Findings are no longer fitted to the same data they are judged on. Segments that fail confirmation are reported as unverified.
- `depth`: The acquisition spend request is behind approval. It enables acquisition cost and payback, which a true retention-versus-acquisition comparison needs, and it adds new data access.
- `range`: Decision analysis (break-even, tornado sensitivity, flip condition) turns the deck into a choice under stated uncertainty. It adds no slides beyond the cap.
- `range`: Causal labeling from epidemiology keeps leaders from funding a driver that is only correlated with churn, since no experiment is possible.
- `range`: The red team uses Analysis of Competing Hypotheses, run by existing staff. It exposes the strongest case against the recommendation before the meeting. It requires a staff member with permission to see the data.
- `range`: The pyramid principle and a ghost deck make the argument readable from headlines alone in the meeting.
- `depth`: The methods-and-reconciliation note is behind approval. It makes the analysis auditable without exceeding 12 slides, and it is extra output the task did not request.
- Skipped: no lens was skipped. I did not use the hard-target move because the task sets no quantitative improvement bar.
- Owner actions:
  - Share the raw customer and revenue exports.
  - Approve or decline the acquisition spend request.
  - Approve or decline the methods note.
  - Name the reviewer and the red-team staff member, and confirm they may see customer and revenue data.
